exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect ischaemic colitis over infectious colitis? — Left‑sided crampy pain with sudden onset, recent hypotensive episode, and absence of fever.
A patient with atrial fibrillation presents with bloody diarrhea; what is your next diagnostic step? — Obtain urgent colonoscopy or CT if colonoscopy unsafe to look for ischaemic changes.
How does low‑flow state cause colonic injury? — Reduced arterial perfusion leads to mucosal hypoxia, edema, and eventual necrosis if not restored.
When should you start empirical antibiotics in suspected ischaemic colitis? — When perforation, peritonitis, or systemic sepsis is present, because bacterial translocation is likely.
Why are vasoconstrictive agents contraindicated in this condition? — They worsen colonic hypoperfusion, increasing the risk of transmural necrosis.
What imaging finding distinguishes severe ischaemic colitis from mild disease? — Presence of pneumatosis intestinalis or portal venous gas indicates transmural injury.

Explain how sickle cell disease can precipitate ischaemic colitis in an African hospital. — Sickled red cells occlude mesenteric microvasculature during vaso‑occlusive crises, causing low‑flow ischemia.
What long‑term measures reduce recurrence risk? — Control cardiovascular risk factors, maintain hydration, and manage cardiac arrhythmias.
ai.title: Ischaemic Colitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Ischaemic colitis is colonic inflammation caused by reduced blood flow, ranging from mild mucosal injury to transmural necrosis. Diagnosis relies on clinical clues and limited imaging, often without advanced tests. Management focuses on supportive care, treating the underlying cause, and early recognition of complications.

b: Acute abdominal pain with bloody diarrhea
Risk factors: atherosclerosis, hypotension, cardiac failure, hypercoagulable states
sections.p: A segmental colonic inflammation due to insufficient arterial perfusion, most often affecting watershed zones. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by colonoscopy or contrast imaging when available.

t.b: Identifies risk factors and typical presentation; guides urgency of further work‑up
Excludes infectious colitis; presence of leukocytes supports inflammation
Shows segmental erythema, ulceration, or pale mucosa; biopsy rules out infection or IBD

t.a: CT abdomen with contrast (or plain X‑ray if CT unavailable)
t.b: Detects colonic wall thickening, pneumatosis, or portal venous gas indicating severe disease

b: Mild: limited mucosal injury, no systemic signs
Moderate: transmural edema, mild tachycardia, hemoglobin drop <2 g/dL
Severe/fulminant: peritonitis, perforation, portal venous gas, hemodynamic instability
sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical course and imaging findings, guiding management intensity.

b: Low‑flow states: severe dehydration, sepsis, heart failure, shock
Arterial emboli/thrombosis: atrial fibrillation, atherosclerotic plaque
Hypercoagulable conditions: HIV, sickle cell disease, antiphospholipid syndrome
Medications: vasoconstrictors, digitalis overdose
Infective vasculitis: severe malaria, disseminated TB
sections.p: Ischaemia results from arterial occlusion, low flow states, or venous outflow obstruction. In low‑resource settings, additional contributors are common.

b: Pain often post‑prandial and improves with rest
Bloody diarrhea may be profuse or intermittent
Fever and leukocytosis suggest more extensive disease
sections.p: Patients usually present with sudden left‑sided abdominal cramping followed by bright red or maroon stools, sometimes mixed with mucus.
Select tests answer key clinical questions; when a test is unavailable, rely on bedside assessment and basic labs.

t.b: Detects anemia and leukocytosis; falling hemoglobin signals ongoing bleed
Elevated >2 mmol/L indicates tissue hypoperfusion and higher mortality
Guides fluid replacement and identifies acute kidney injury from hypovolemia
Shows colonic dilatation or pneumoperitoneum when perforation is suspected

b: Peritoneal signs (rigidity, rebound tenderness)
Persistent tachycardia >120 bpm despite fluids
Drop in hemoglobin >2 g/dL within 24 h
Portal venous gas or pneumatosis intestinalis on imaging
sections.p: Prompt recognition of severe disease prevents mortality.

b: Aggressive IV crystalloid replacement (goal MAP ≥65 mmHg)
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) if perforation or sepsis suspected
Avoid vasoconstrictive drugs (e.g., ergotamines, phenylephrine)
Consider anticoagulation reversal if drug‑induced thrombosis
Surgical consult early for signs of perforation or uncontrolled bleeding
sections.p: Treat the precipitating cause, provide supportive care, and monitor for deterioration.

b: Control hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidaemia
Encourage adequate hydration, especially during diarrheal illnesses
Review cardiac rhythm disorders and optimise anticoagulation
Schedule colonoscopic surveillance if chronic ischemic changes persist
sections.p: After acute recovery, address underlying vascular risk factors and educate on early warning signs.

Inflammatory bowel disease – chronic course, extra‑intestinal manifestations
Diverticulitis with bleeding – localized left‑lower quadrant pain, often without extensive colonic edema
sections.p: Conditions sharing abdominal pain and bloody stool can mislead clinicians.

Absence of pneumatosis on plain X‑ray does not exclude severe ischemia
Mild lactate rise may be missed if sample delayed
sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal despite serious disease.

Persistent vomiting with inability to maintain blood pressure
